---
title: "Gradient Descent"
description: "An iterative optimization method that updates parameters in the direction of decreasing loss."
term: "Gradient Descent"
letter: "G"
category: "Machine Learning"
difficulty: "Beginner"

## Simple explanation

Gradient descent improves model parameters by repeatedly measuring how
the loss changes and taking a step in the direction that locally reduces
it.

## Technical explanation

For parameters $\theta$, loss $L(\theta)$, and learning rate $\eta$, a
basic update is $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta\nabla_\theta L(\theta_t)$.
Batch, stochastic, and mini-batch variants differ in how much training
data is used to estimate each gradient. Optimizers such as momentum and
Adam modify the update rule.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Gradient-based optimization trains many machine-learning models.
Learning-rate choice, noisy gradients, loss geometry, and data order
affect convergence, stability, and compute requirements.

## How it works

At each step, calculate the loss gradient at current parameters, scale
the update by a learning rate, and move parameters opposite the
gradient. Repeat until a stopping criterion or training budget is met.
The method may reach a local solution or fail to converge depending on
the objective and configuration.

## Practical example

A neural network calculates its training loss and gradients for a
mini-batch. An optimizer updates its weights, then processes another
batch and repeats the procedure.

## Common misconceptions

- Gradient descent does not guarantee finding a global minimum.
- A larger learning rate is not always faster; it can overshoot or
  destabilize training.
- The loss may fluctuate between updates, especially with mini-batch
  gradients.
